lead: A pulse radar sends a pulse, listens, and sends the next one. The pulse repetition frequency (PRF) sets how long it listens, and so the longest range it can measure without mixing up one pulse's echo with the next. PRF also sets the average power and how often the Doppler shift is sampled, so it is one of the first numbers chosen in any radar design. Air traffic, weather and airborne fire-control radars all pick their PRF around this compromise.
prereq: You need R = c t / 2 and the range resolution cτ/2 from Radar principle, block diagram and frequency bands.

blocks.text: PRF is the number of pulses sent per second. The time from one pulse to the next is the pulse repetition interval, T<sub>r</sub> = 1/PRF. The transmitter is on for τ of each interval, and the receiver listens for the rest, T<sub>r</sub> − τ. An echo is placed correctly only if it returns before the next pulse leaves:

Runamb = c Tr / 2 = c / (2 PRF)
Here Runamb is the maximum unambiguous range in m; Tr is in s; PRF is in Hz; c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Because τ is far shorter than Tr, the small loss of listening time is usually neglected.
Turned round, a radar that must place targets correctly out to R<sub>max</sub> needs PRF ≤ c/(2R<sub>max</sub>): 150 km allows at most 1 kHz.

The fraction of time the transmitter is on is the duty cycle, d = τ/T<sub>r</sub> = τ·PRF. The average power is P<sub>av</sub> = P<sub>t</sub>·d, with P<sub>t</sub> the peak power. A 1 MW, 1 µs radar at 1 kHz has d = 0.001 and P<sub>av</sub> = 1 kW. The cooling and the power supply are sized for P<sub>av</sub>; the tube and the duplexer must survive P<sub>t</sub>.
Ten times the PRF gives one tenth of the unambiguous range.

sections.h3: Second-time-around echoes and the blind zone

blocks.text: A target beyond R<sub>unamb</sub> still returns an echo, but it arrives after the next pulse has left. The radar measures delay from the latest pulse, so it shows the target too close. This is a second-time-around (or multiple-time-around) echo:

blocks.where: R<sub>app</sub> is the apparent range; R is the true range; n is the whole number of intervals the echo is late, chosen so that 0 ≤ R<sub>app</sub> < R<sub>unamb</sub>.

blocks.text: The figure draws this for the worked example: a target at 200 km, at a PRF of 1 kHz, shows up at 50 km.
At the near end, the receiver is switched off while the pulse is sent and while the duplexer recovers. Echoes arriving then are lost, so there is a blind zone close to the radar:

blocks.where: R<sub>min</sub> is the minimum range in m; τ is the pulse width and t<sub>rec</sub> the duplexer and receiver recovery time, both in s. A 1 µs pulse alone blinds the first 150 m.

blocks.text: An echo can also be lost in the same way far out, when it arrives exactly while a later pulse is being sent; this is called eclipsing. The receiver timeline is cut into range gates, each one pulse width τ long in time and therefore cτ/2 long in range, and the processor examines each gate separately.

sections.h3: The PRF trade-off and multiple PRFs

blocks.text: PRF also samples the Doppler shift: a radar measuring phase once per pulse can only tell Doppler frequencies apart over a span of one PRF. So:

items: Low PRF (a few hundred hertz to a few kHz): long unambiguous range, but Doppler is badly ambiguous. Used by search and air traffic radars.
High PRF (tens to hundreds of kHz): Doppler is unambiguous for fast targets, but range is heavily ambiguous. Used by airborne pulse Doppler radars to see fast closing targets.
Medium PRF: both are ambiguous, but each only a little, and several PRFs together sort them out.

blocks.text: Multiple PRFs remove the ambiguity. The radar sends bursts at two or more PRFs. A real target folds to a different apparent range at each PRF, but only one true range fits every reading. With two PRFs whose unambiguous ranges are R1 and R2, the pair is unambiguous out to their least common multiple. Staggered PRF, which changes Tr from pulse to pulse, makes second-time-around echoes jump about while true echoes stay put; it also moves the blind speeds of MTI radar. The Doppler side of the trade is in CW and FMCW radar.

examples.question: A radar has PRF = 1000 Hz, pulse width 1 µs and peak power 1 MW. Find T<sub>r</sub>, the duty cycle, the average power, the unambiguous range and the blind range from the pulse alone. A target is really at 200 km: where does the radar show it?
steps: Duty cycle d = τ/T<sub>r</sub> = 1 × 10⁻⁶ / 1 × 10⁻³ = 0.001 (0.1 %); P<sub>av</sub> = 10⁶ × 0.001 = 1 kW.
Blind range from the pulse: cτ/2 = 3 × 10⁸ × 10⁻⁶ / 2 = 150 m.
True range 200 km lies one interval beyond: n = 1, R<sub>app</sub> = 200 − 150 = 50 km.
examples.answer: T<sub>r</sub> = 1 ms, d = 0.001, P<sub>av</sub> = 1 kW, R<sub>unamb</sub> = 150 km, blind range 150 m; the 200 km target is shown at 50 km.

examples.question: The same radar now alternates bursts at 1000 Hz and 1250 Hz. The target appears at 50 km at the first PRF and at 80 km at the second. Find its true range, and the largest range the pair can resolve.
steps: Ranges that fit the first reading: 50, 200, 350, 500 km, … (50 + 150n).
Ranges that fit the second reading: 80, 200, 320, 440 km, … (80 + 120n).
The first value in both lists is 200 km, so the target is at 200 km.
The lists repeat their match every least common multiple of 150 and 120 km, which is 600 km. Check: 600/150 = 4 and 600/120 = 5, both whole.
examples.answer: The target is at 200 km; the two PRFs together are unambiguous out to 600 km, four times the range of the lower PRF alone.

traps: Writing R<sub>unamb</sub> = c/PRF. The echo must go out and back within one interval, so it is c/(2 PRF).
Using τ where T<sub>r</sub> belongs. τ sets the blind zone and the range resolution; T<sub>r</sub> sets the unambiguous range.
Treating a second-time-around echo as noise. It is a real target, shown at R − nR<sub>unamb</sub>.
Saying a high PRF is always better. It improves Doppler coverage and average power, but shortens the unambiguous range.
Sizing the cooling for peak power. Heat follows the average power, P<sub>t</sub> × duty cycle.

quiz.q: Define PRF and give its relation to the pulse repetition interval.
quiz.a: PRF is the number of pulses sent per second; the pulse repetition interval is T<sub>r</sub> = 1/PRF.

quiz.q: Write the blind (minimum) range in terms of the pulse width and the recovery time.
Why does the unambiguous range formula contain a factor 2?
quiz.a: The path to the target and back is 2R, so the delay is 2R/c; this must be no longer than T<sub>r</sub>, giving R ≤ cT<sub>r</sub>/2.

quiz.q: A radar has PRF = 2000 Hz. Find R<sub>unamb</sub>.
A radar has peak power 500 kW, pulse width 2 µs and PRF 500 Hz. Find the duty cycle and the average power.
A target is at 120 km and the PRF is 2000 Hz. What range is shown, and how could the operator tell it is not a real target at that range?
quiz.a: R<sub>unamb</sub> = 75 km, so it is shown at 120 − 75 = 45 km. Changing the PRF moves it (at 1500 Hz, R<sub>unamb</sub> = 100 km and it appears at 20 km), while a real target at 45 km stays at 45 km.

quiz.q: Compare low and high PRF for range and Doppler ambiguity.
quiz.a: Low PRF: long unambiguous range but ambiguous Doppler. High PRF: unambiguous Doppler for fast targets but short unambiguous range. Medium PRF is partly ambiguous in both.

quiz.q: What is the highest PRF a radar may use if it must place targets correctly out to 250 km?

beyond: Pulse compression lets a long pulse carry a lot of energy and still give the fine resolution of a short one, so PRF and pulse width can be chosen more freely. Airborne radars cycle through sets of medium PRFs (for example, three of eight) so that every target is seen unambiguously in at least some of them. Search for "medium PRF ambiguity resolution", "Chinese remainder theorem radar" and "range-Doppler ambiguity" to go further.
